answer_1.quote: We study appropriate reliance close to the actual decision that users have to make on the ground: whether or not to rely on a model output. We study this question in the context of physicians deciding when to rely on Machine Translation (MT) in an emergency room when communicating discharge instructions to a patient who does not speak their language.
datasets: de-identified Emergency Department (ED) discharge instructions that were written between the years 2016 to 2021 at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF)
answer_1.outputs: automatically translated into simplified Chinese by Google Translate

answer_2.quote: COMET-QE achieves an accuracy of 66% and 73% on detecting adequate and clinically insignificant translations, respectively.

answer_4.quote: Three bilingual physicians independently annotated each MT output along two dimensions: translation adequacy and clinical risk.
answer_4.guideline: Adequacy was defined as whether the Chinese translation accurately conveyed the meaning of the English source text. Physicians rated clinical risk based on the translation presented to them according to five categories: clinically insignificant, mildly clinically significant, moderately clinically significant, highly clinically significant, and life-threatening.
